title: Justice for all
hook: the good of all includes standing for the wronged

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama: force only when every other means has failed. Your line was peace first. Did you try a gentler way before a sharp one? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

The Sikh ardas, the standing prayer at the end of a service, closes on a wish for the whole world. Tere bhane sarbat da bhala: in your will, the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. Not the good of the people in the room. Everyone. It's a lovely wish to say aloud. It's also a hard one to mean. Because once the good of all is the goal, someone being trampled is no longer somebody else's business. Guru Nanak once watched a city being trampled, and what he said about it is where today begins.
screen: `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` → `NOT JUST US. EVERYONE.` → `A CITY TRAMPLED.`

segments.voice: First, the cry. When Babur's armies swept in, Guru Nanak, tradition says, saw the slaughter with his own eyes. His hymns about it are called the Babarvani. In one, in Raag Asa, he speaks straight to God. In paraphrase: such suffering, such crying out, and did You feel no pain? He doesn't soften it. He describes the women whose hair was once braided for weddings, now dragged and shamed. A hymn can be a protest. Second, naming it plainly. In another of these hymns, in Raag Tilang, he calls the invading host a wedding party of sin, and says he will speak the word of truth, because the time for truth has come. No flattery of the powerful. Justice starts with refusing to call a wrong anything else. Third, the good of all. That's the bridge to sarbat da bhala. If the good of all is real, it includes the people being wronged, and it lays a claim on whoever sees it. Sikh memory keeps stories, from the Gurus to the Khalsa, of standing up for people who weren't their own. Fourth, what standing looks like when the stakes are small. Few of us will ever face an army. But someone is talked over in a meeting. Someone gets the cruel nickname. Someone's rent goes unfixed because they won't complain. Standing for them might mean a word, a witness, a phone call, a seat beside them. Guru Nanak had no army to send. He had a hymn, and he sang it. One true sentence on someone's behalf is still within anyone's reach.
screen: `THE BABARVANI: DID YOU FEEL NO PAIN?` · `TILANG: SAY THE WRONG BY ITS NAME.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA INCLUDES THE WRONGED.` · `A WORD, A WITNESS, A SEAT BESIDE.` · then, large: `STAND FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is being treated unfairly, near you or far away. Don't rush past their face. Breathe in, and let yourself see what they're carrying. Breathe out, and ask: what is one true thing I could say or do for them? A message, a word to the right person, simply showing up. Let one action become clear, small enough to do today. The bell holds the time.
Justice for all. Sarbat da bhala, the good of all, includes standing for the wronged, as Guru Nanak did when he cried out against Babur's slaughter. Today's word.
Your line: stand for others. Today, when you see someone treated unfairly, don't wait to be the second voice. Say one true sentence on their side. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs end the ardas with sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and remember Guru Nanak's Babarvani hymns as a protest against the suffering of ordinary people.

what it means: the good of all, sarbat da bhala, includes standing for whoever is wronged.
